opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to be clear about what a model of the world actually is. To have a model of the world, you'd have to be able to predict what will happen, what the consequences of your actions will be. Large language models aren't doing that. They're predicting what a person would say. They're mimicking people who have models of the world, but that's not the same thing as having one yourself.

The key test is whether you can be surprised. If you have a real model of the world, you make a prediction, something happens in the world, and you find out you were wrong, and you adjust. That's learning from experience. But a language model doesn't have that. It predicts the next token in a text, but there's no sense in which it's predicting what will happen in the world as a result of what it does. It doesn't take an action and then see what follows. There's no feedback from the world itself, only from what people wrote.

And without a goal, without something that counts as right or wrong in terms of the consequences in the world, there's no ground truth. In reinforcement learning, there's a right thing to do, the thing that gets you reward. That gives you something to learn about, something to be correct about. With large language models, what's "right" is just whatever a person would have said next, and that's a very different thing.

So I'd say they have a model of what people say, which is impressive in its way, but calling it a model of the world goes too far. The world is what you interact with, and they don't really interact with it. Mimicry is not understanding, and I think the whole approach is, in a sense, a detour. The real path to intelligence is through experience: an agent acting, observing what happens, and learning from that.

r001.rationale: It says language models predict what a person would say, which is not the same as predicting what will happen in the world.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from experience as an agent acting, observing what follows, and adjusting based on the result.

r003.rationale: It describes language models as mimicking people and predicting what a person would say next, but does not characterize training on examples of human behavior as implicitly prescribing imitation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back on the premise a little. People say these models have a world model, and I'd ask: what is a world model? To me, a model of the world is something that lets you predict what will happen. You take an action, and the model tells you what the consequences will be. That's what the world is: it's the thing that responds to what you do.

Now, what do large language models predict? They predict what a person would say next. That's not the same thing. That's a model of people, of text, of what humans have said. It's not a model of what will happen in the world if you do something. There's no action, there's no consequence, and critically, there's no surprise. When you have a real world model and you make a prediction and it's wrong, the world tells you. You get a signal. You learn from that. These systems don't have that. They can't be surprised by the world, because they're not predicting the world. They're predicting the next token, and they're trained on what the token actually was in the data, and then that's over.

So I'd say it's mimicry. It's a very impressive kind of mimicry, and you can get a lot out of it, because a tremendous amount of knowledge is encoded in what people have written. But you're borrowing the world model that the humans had. You're not building one yourself. And the trouble is that the humans' knowledge is where it stops. You have no way to go beyond it, no way to find out when it's wrong, no way to continue learning from experience. That's the big thing that's missing. Intelligence, as I think of it, is about an agent that has goals, that acts, and that learns from the consequences of its actions. Large language models aren't doing that. They have no goal in the world; they have a goal of matching the text, which is a different thing entirely.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes predicting what a person will say next from predicting what will happen in the world after an action.

r002.rationale: It says a world model learns from the signal received when its predictions about the consequences of actions are wrong.

r003.rationale: It describes training to predict human text and match the observed next token as mimicry of what people have said.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would question what we mean by a model of the world. Do we mean something that predicts what a person will say about the world, or something that predicts what will happen when you take an action? Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

Language can convey a great deal of knowledge. So I wouldn’t say that a system trained on language can’t learn anything about the world. But its training objective is to predict language. If people systematically misunderstand something, reproducing that misunderstanding can be the correct answer for its objective. There’s no independent check against what actually happens.

The kind of world model I’m interested in is one an agent can use to predict the consequences of its actions, and then improve through experience when those predictions are wrong. Mimicking human language may help you get started. What I question is whether that alone gives you the learning process we ultimately need.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes predicting what a person will say from predicting what will happen when an agent acts, and says the two are not the same.

r002.rationale: It says an agent predicts the consequences of its actions and improves through experience when those predictions are wrong, conveying learning from action outcomes.

r003.rationale: It describes the objective as predicting language and discusses mimicking language, but does not characterize training examples of human behavior as implicitly prescribing imitation of that behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t doubt that they learn something about the world. Language contains a great deal of information about the world. The question is what kind of model they learn, and whether it’s sufficient for an agent to act intelligently.

If you train a system to predict what a person will say, then that’s what you’re directly training it to do. You’re not directly training it to predict what will happen if it takes an action. Those predictions can overlap, but they’re different things. A person can describe how a physical process works without being able to predict it accurately, and a language model can learn that description.

What I want from a world model is something an agent can use to reason about the consequences of its actions: if I do this, what will I observe, and what reward will I receive? And then it should be able to test those predictions and improve them through experience. Learning from human language could contribute to that. But success at imitating language doesn’t, by itself, establish that you’ve learned such a model.

r001.rationale: The response says predicting what a person will say is a different objective from predicting what will happen after an action, and that language imitation alone does not establish a usable world model.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting an action’s observations and reward, then testing and improving those predictions through experience.

r003.rationale: It says training a system to predict what a person will say directly trains it to do that, conveying imitation of human language behavior.
